questions.question: Analyse the reasons why the Muslims of India came to demand a separate homeland. To what extent was the experience of Congress rule between 1937 and 1939 responsible? [8]
questions.model_answer:
The demand grew out of a long process rather than a single cause. From the late nineteenth century Sir Syed Ahmad Khan argued that Muslims formed a separate nation with their own religion, language, culture and history, an argument later developed into the Two-Nation Theory. Constitutional experience reinforced this: the grant of separate electorates in 1909 recognised Muslims as a distinct political community, and the collapse of the Lucknow Pact showed that cooperation with Congress was fragile. Iqbal gave the idea territorial form at Allahabad in 1930, and the Lahore Resolution of 1940 made it official policy.

The Congress ministries of 1937-39 were, however, decisive in converting an idea into a mass demand. After the Government of India Act 1935 Congress won power in most provinces and, having refused coalition with the Muslim League, governed alone. Muslims complained of the Wardha education scheme, the promotion of Hindi over Urdu, the singing of Bande Matram, the flying of the Congress flag over public buildings, and bias in appointments and in the handling of communal disputes. The League collected these complaints in the Pirpur and Shareef reports. When the ministries resigned in 1939 the League observed a Day of Deliverance.

In assessment, Congress rule was not the origin of the demand, since the intellectual and constitutional foundations were already laid. Its importance is that it supplied proof. It showed ordinary Muslims what a Hindu-majority government would mean in practice, transformed the League from an elite body into a mass party, and made the argument for a separate state persuasive to people who had previously been indifferent. It is therefore best described as the decisive catalyst rather than the root cause.

questions.question: Analyse the importance of the Indus river system to Pakistan. Why is the management of water resources such a serious challenge for the country? [8]
questions.model_answer:
The Indus and its tributaries, the Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi and Sutlej, are the foundation of Pakistan's existence. Around ninety per cent of agriculture depends on irrigation drawn from the system, and agriculture in turn supplies employment for a large part of the population, raw materials for the textile and sugar industries, and a major share of exports. The barrages and link canals form one of the largest contiguous irrigation networks in the world. Dams at Tarbela and Mangla also generate a substantial share of national electricity and store water for the dry season. The rivers deposit alluvium that keeps the Punjab and Sindh plains fertile, and they sustain the mangrove forests and fisheries of the delta.

Management is difficult for several reasons. Flow is highly seasonal, concentrated in the summer monsoon and snowmelt, so water is abundant when it is not needed and scarce when it is. Storage capacity is limited and falling, because Tarbela and Mangla are silting up. Water is shared with India under the Indus Water Treaty of 1960, which gave India the three eastern rivers, so Pakistan depends on the western rivers and disputes over Indian upstream projects recur. Internally, the provinces disagree over their shares, particularly between Punjab and Sindh. Canal irrigation without adequate drainage has caused widespread waterlogging and salinity, taking land out of production. Losses through unlined canals are large, flood irrigation is wasteful, and water is heavily under-priced so there is little incentive to conserve it. Climate change is now adding glacier melt, more erratic monsoons and more frequent floods and droughts.

The conclusion is that the Indus system is both Pakistan's greatest natural asset and its greatest vulnerability, since almost every sector of the economy is exposed to a single, contested and increasingly unreliable source.

questions.question: Analyse the constitutional development of Pakistan between 1947 and 1973. Why did it take so long for the country to produce a lasting constitution? [8]
questions.model_answer:
At independence Pakistan governed itself under the Government of India Act 1935 as adapted by the Independence Act, an arrangement intended to be temporary. The Objectives Resolution of 1949 set out the guiding principles, declaring the sovereignty of Allah, democracy, equality and social justice, fundamental rights and protection for minorities. Agreement on a full constitution proved far harder. The first Constituent Assembly worked for nine years before the 1956 Constitution declared Pakistan an Islamic Republic with a parliamentary system. It lasted barely two years before being abrogated by martial law in 1958. The 1962 Constitution introduced a presidential system with strong executive powers and the indirect Basic Democracies system of election; it too fell in 1969. The 1973 Constitution, framed under Bhutto with unusually broad political agreement, restored a parliamentary federal system with a bicameral legislature and remains in force.

Several reasons explain the delay. The most serious was the dispute over representation between East and West Pakistan: East Pakistan had the larger population but the west held political and military power, and the awkward compromises of parity and the One Unit scheme satisfied neither. There was persistent disagreement over the role of Islam in the state and over the powers of the provinces against the centre. Political parties were weak and unstable, ministries changed frequently, and the early deaths of Jinnah in 1948 and Liaquat Ali Khan in 1951 removed the leaders with the authority to force a settlement. Meanwhile the civil service and the army grew strong relative to elected politicians, and repeated interventions by governors-general and later by the army interrupted the process.

In assessment, the delay reflected genuine and unresolved questions about what kind of state Pakistan was to be, compounded by a weak political system that lacked the stability to answer them.

questions.question: Evaluate the main problems facing agriculture in Pakistan. What steps could be taken to increase agricultural productivity? [7]
questions.model_answer:
Pakistani agriculture suffers from persistently low yields per hectare compared with other countries growing the same crops. Landholdings are small and fragmented because land is divided between sons at inheritance, which makes mechanisation uneconomic. Many farmers are tenants with no security of tenure, so they have little incentive to improve the land. Water is used inefficiently through flood irrigation and unlined canals, and inadequate drainage has caused waterlogging and salinity across large areas of Punjab and Sindh. Farmers often use poor-quality seed and either too little fertiliser or the wrong kind, and lack access to credit except from moneylenders charging high rates. Pest attacks, especially on cotton, cause heavy losses. Storage and transport are poor, so a significant part of the harvest is wasted before sale, and middlemen take much of the price. Floods, drought and increasingly erratic monsoons add severe risk.

Improvement requires action on several fronts. Land reform and consolidation of holdings would allow more efficient use of machinery. Lining canals and introducing drip and sprinkler irrigation, together with realistic water pricing, would cut waste. Tube wells and improved drainage can tackle waterlogging and salinity. Farmers need reliable access to certified high-yield seed, correct fertiliser and affordable credit through agricultural banks rather than moneylenders. Agricultural extension services and farmer training spread better techniques, and research into drought and pest-resistant varieties is essential. Better farm-to-market roads, cold storage and regulated markets would reduce waste and give farmers a fairer price. Crop insurance would help farmers survive floods and droughts. Taken together these measures address the underlying causes rather than the symptoms, but they require sustained government investment and political will.

questions.question: Evaluate the obstacles to industrial development in Pakistan. How might the country strengthen its industrial base? [7]
questions.model_answer:
Pakistan's industry remains narrow and vulnerable. It is heavily concentrated on cotton textiles, so a bad cotton harvest or a fall in world textile prices damages the whole economy, and there has been little movement into higher-value manufacturing such as engineering, chemicals or electronics. Energy shortages and load-shedding interrupt production and raise costs, and much industrial machinery is old and inefficient. Capital for investment is scarce and interest rates are high. The workforce is large but often lacks technical and vocational skills. Bureaucratic procedures, unreliable enforcement of contracts and frequent changes in policy discourage both domestic and foreign investors. Transport bottlenecks and port congestion add to costs, and political instability and security concerns have reduced foreign direct investment. Because most exports are low-value and imports include expensive fuel and machinery, the country runs a persistent trade deficit.

Strengthening the base means addressing these directly. Reliable and affordable energy, including investment in hydel, solar and coal generation, is the first requirement. Diversifying beyond textiles into engineering goods, food processing, pharmaceuticals and information technology would reduce dependence on a single sector. Expanding technical and vocational training would supply the skilled workers that modern industry needs. Special economic zones and simplified, stable regulation would attract investment, and CPEC infrastructure offers improved transport and access to regional markets. Support for small and medium enterprises, which employ large numbers, would broaden growth, and moving exports up the value chain from raw cotton and yarn towards finished garments would raise earnings from the same output. Progress depends on continuity of policy across governments, which has historically been the weakest point.

questions.question: Evaluate the problems created by Pakistan's rapid population growth. What measures could help the country manage them? [7]
questions.model_answer:
Pakistan's population has grown very rapidly since independence and remains one of the fastest-growing in the region. The growth is driven by a high birth rate, falling death rates as health care improved, early marriage, low female literacy, and the preference for large families in rural areas where children are an economic asset and old-age security.

The problems this creates are wide-ranging. Schools and hospitals cannot expand fast enough, so class sizes rise and health care per person falls. The labour force grows faster than the economy can create jobs, producing high unemployment and underemployment, particularly among young people. Land is subdivided into ever smaller holdings, reducing agricultural efficiency. Demand rises for water, food and energy that are already in short supply, forcing up imports. Cities receive heavy migration, so katchi abadis spread and water, sanitation and transport come under strain. Pressure on land and fuel contributes to deforestation and pollution, and a very young dependent population limits national saving and investment.

Management requires long-term social change rather than short-term measures. Female education is the most effective single intervention, since birth rates fall consistently as girls stay in school longer. Family planning services, and awareness campaigns that work with religious and community leaders rather than against them, help couples space births. Raising the age of marriage, improving child health so that parents do not need large families for security, and providing old-age pensions all reduce the incentive for large families. Investment in vocational training and job creation can turn a large young population into a demographic advantage rather than a burden. Rural development that provides jobs, schools and clinics in the villages would also slow the flow of migrants into the cities.
